p4-6.qa: Vendor transfers were tied to ComponentPro, and in [2024] a vendor hardened their server and broke our connection. Per-vendor configuration enabled gradual rollout and instant rollback.
Result framing: "a library change went from a code rewrite to a configuration change", which is the kind of leverage interviewers remember.
f: How did you prove it was better?
Library swaps became config changes, and vendor failures dropped.
What would you improve next?
Retire ComponentPro and add synthetic transfer checks.
wv: I improve systems so future changes are cheap.

p4-17.a: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.|Together they hide details, model contracts, reuse code and swap behaviour at runtime, for example ISftpClient with three providers.
p4-17.qa: The four OOP principles are encapsulation (bundle data with behaviour and hide state), abstraction (expose what, hide how), inheritance (reuse via is-a) and polymorphism (one interface, many implementations). Together they let us hide details, define contracts and swap behaviour, as with ISftpClient and three providers.
i: Modern C# favours composition and interfaces over deep inheritance.
SOLID builds on these principles.
Example map: Shipment.MarkDelivered (encapsulation), ISftpClient (abstraction/polymorphism), SftpClientBase (inheritance).
Interview tip: give one example per principle from your own code, not textbook animals and shapes.
f: Which is most important?
Encapsulation, because it protects invariants.
Is C# purely OOP?
No, it's multi-paradigm with strong functional features (LINQ, records, pattern matching).

p4-18.a: Bundle data with the methods that change it and hide internal state behind a public surface (private fields, properties, methods that enforce rules).|Example: a Shipment exposes `MarkDelivered()` that validates the status, instead of a public settable Status.
p4-18.qa: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that change it and hides internal state behind a controlled public surface, so invariants can't be broken. A Shipment exposes MarkDelivered() which checks the current status and sets the delivery time, instead of a public settable Status.
i: Private setters, readonly fields, and validation in methods.
Rich domain models vs anemic models (data bags with logic elsewhere).
Expose collections as IReadOnlyCollection.
f: Encapsulation vs abstraction?
Encapsulation hides state and protects it; abstraction hides complexity behind a simple contract.
Can EF Core map private setters?
Yes, it uses backing fields.

p4-19.a: A class derives from a base class to reuse and extend its behaviour (an is-a relationship).|Example: SftpClientBase holds retry and logging; each provider class inherits it.|Prefer composition when the relationship is has-a or behaviour varies a lot.
p4-19.qa: Inheritance lets a class derive from a base class to reuse and extend its behaviour (is-a). SftpClientBase holds retry and logging, and each provider class inherits it and implements library-specific calls. I prefer composition when the relationship isn't truly is-a or behaviour varies independently.
i: C# supports single class inheritance and multiple interface implementation.
Template method pattern: base defines the algorithm, subclasses fill steps.
Fragile base class problem: base changes break subclasses.
Default interface methods (C# 8) add some shared behaviour to interfaces.
f: Why no multiple inheritance?
To avoid the diamond problem; interfaces give the flexibility instead.
Abstract class vs interface?
Abstract classes share code and state; interfaces define contracts and allow multiple implementation.

p4-20.a: One interface, many implementations: the method that runs is chosen at runtime (virtual/override, interfaces) or at compile time (overloading).|Example: code calls `ISftpClient.UploadAsync`, and Rebex or SSH.NET runs depending on configuration.
p4-20.qa: Polymorphism means one interface, many implementations: the method that runs is chosen at runtime through virtual/override or interfaces, or at compile time through overloading and generics. Code calls ISftpClient.UploadAsync and the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation runs.
i: Runtime dispatch uses virtual method tables; the JIT can devirtualize sealed or known types (and dynamic PGO helps).
Parametric polymorphism: generics.
Pattern matching offers an alternative for closed hierarchies.
Example: an INotifier interface with EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier; a loop over IEnumerable<INotifier> sends through all without knowing types.
f: Overloading vs overriding?
Overloading is compile-time by signature; overriding is runtime by actual type.
What is dynamic PGO?
Profile-guided optimisation at runtime, on by default since .NET 8, which can devirtualize hot calls.

p4-21.a: Expose what something does and hide how it does it; interfaces and abstract classes model the essential contract.|Callers depend on ISftpClient without knowing any library details.
p4-21.qa: Abstraction exposes what something does and hides how; interfaces and abstract classes model the essential contract. Callers depend on ISftpClient without knowing any library details.
i: Good abstractions are small and stable; leaky abstractions expose implementation details (library exceptions).
We mapped provider exceptions to our own to avoid leaking.
Don't abstract too early; wait for a second implementation or a testing need.
Abstraction levels: repository hides SQL, ISftpClient hides libraries, the service layer hides workflow; each layer talks only to the one below.
f: What is a leaky abstraction?
One where callers must understand the hidden implementation to use it correctly.
Abstraction vs interface keyword?
Abstraction is the concept; interfaces are one way to express it.

p4-22.a: A class is the blueprint (the type definition); an object is an instance created from it at runtime, with its own state.
p4-22.qa: A class is the blueprint (type definition with fields, properties and methods); an object is an instance created from it at runtime with its own state on the heap. Many objects can come from one class.
i: Static members belong to the type, not instances.
Records and structs are also types; structs create values, not heap objects (unless boxed).
Object header holds sync block and method table pointer.
Records add value-based equality and with-expressions; structs are copied by value; classes are referenced.
f: Where are objects stored?
On the managed heap; references point to them.
What's a static class?
A class that can't be instantiated and holds only static members.

p4-23.a: Overloading: same method name with different parameters in the same class, resolved at compile time.|Overriding: a derived class replaces a virtual base method with the same signature, resolved at runtime.
p4-23.qa: Overloading is the same method name with different parameters in one class, resolved at compile time; overriding is a derived class replacing a virtual base method with the same signature, resolved at runtime by the actual object type.
i: Return type alone can't distinguish overloads.
Overload resolution picks the best match; optional parameters and params can create ambiguity.
Covariant return types (C# 9) let overrides return a more derived type.
Overload resolution happens at compile time on static types: passing an object-typed variable picks the object overload even if it holds a string.
f: Can you override a non-virtual method?
No; you can only hide it with new.
Can static methods be overridden?
No; static abstract interface members are a different feature for generic math.

p4-24.a: `virtual` in the base class marks a method as replaceable; `override` in the derived class supplies the new implementation.|A call through a base-class reference runs the override (runtime dispatch).
p4-24.qa: virtual in the base class marks a method as replaceable; override in the derived class supplies the new implementation, and a call through a base reference runs the override because dispatch uses the runtime type.
i: abstract methods are implicitly virtual and must be overridden.
base.Method() calls the base implementation from an override.
Calling virtual methods in constructors is risky: the derived override runs before the derived constructor finishes.
Virtual calls go through the method table (vtable); the JIT can devirtualize when the exact type is known, e.g. sealed classes.
f: Are methods virtual by default in C#?
No, unlike Java; you must mark them.
Why avoid virtual calls in constructors?
Derived fields may not be initialised yet.

p4-25.a: `override` replaces a virtual method, so base-typed references call the derived version.|`new` hides the base method (method hiding): which one runs depends on the reference's declared type, a common source of bugs.|Use override for polymorphism; use new only for deliberate shadowing.
p4-25.qa: override replaces a virtual method so base-typed references call the derived version; new hides the base method (method hiding), so which runs depends on the declared reference type, a common source of bugs.
i: The compiler warns (CS0108) when hiding without new.
Hiding breaks polymorphism; use rarely, e.g. when a base library adds a conflicting member.
Real-world use: hiding happens accidentally when a base library adds a member with the same name; treat CS0108 as an error.
f: When is new useful?
To intentionally shadow a member you can't change, with a clear reason.
What does the CS0108 warning mean?
You're hiding an inherited member without saying new.

p4-26.a: A sealed class cannot be inherited (string is sealed); a sealed override stops further overriding down the chain.|Use it for design intent and safety; it also lets the JIT devirtualize calls.
p4-26.qa: A sealed class can't be inherited (string is sealed); a sealed override stops further overriding down the chain. I use it to express design intent and safety, and it lets the JIT devirtualize calls for a small performance gain.
i: Many analyzers (CA1852) suggest sealing internal types that aren't inherited.
Sealed records are common for DTOs and messages.
Sealing public library types is a compatibility decision.
Records can be sealed and their ToString can be sealed (C# 10) so derived records keep it.
f: Why is string sealed?
For immutability and security guarantees and performance.
Can you seal a method that isn't an override?
No, sealed applies to overrides only.

p4-27.a: Stack: per-thread LIFO memory for method frames, locals and value types; very fast and freed when the method returns.|Heap: shared managed memory for objects (reference types), cleaned by the GC.|A value type lives where it is declared: as a field of an object it is on the heap.
p4-27.qa: The stack is per-thread LIFO memory for method frames, locals and value types, very fast and freed when the method returns; the heap is shared managed memory for objects (reference types), cleaned by the GC. Value types live where they're declared: inside a heap object's fields, they're on the heap.
i: Default stack size about 1 MB per thread (Windows main thread); deep recursion causes StackOverflowException, which can't be caught.
stackalloc and Span<T> allow stack buffers.
Large objects (85,000 bytes or more) go to the Large Object Heap.
Captured locals in lambdas or async methods move to heap objects.
f: Are structs always on the stack?
No; fields of a class, array elements, boxed values and captured variables live on the heap.
What is the LOH?
The Large Object Heap for objects of 85 KB or more, collected with Gen 2.

p4-28.a: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (int to object); unboxing casts it back.|It costs an allocation and GC work; avoid it with generics (List<int>, not ArrayList).
p4-28.qa: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (int to object); unboxing casts it back to the exact type. Each box costs an allocation and GC work, so I avoid it with generics (List<int> instead of ArrayList) and by avoiding object parameters for value types.
i: Hidden boxing: string.Format with value types (older), interfaces on structs, non-generic collections, enums in some APIs.
Unboxing to the wrong type throws InvalidCastException.
Interpolated string handlers (C# 10) avoid boxing in many cases.
Generic constraints (where T : struct) and generic interfaces (IEquatable<T>) avoid boxing in comparisons.
f: How do you find boxing?
Allocation profilers or IL inspection (box instructions).
Does calling an interface method on a struct box?
Yes through an interface reference, but not with a constrained generic.

p4-29.a: IDisposable.Dispose releases unmanaged resources (connections, streams, SFTP sessions) deterministically.|`using (var x = ...) { }` calls Dispose at the end of the block, even on exceptions; the C# 8 using declaration `using var x = ...;` disposes at the end of the scope.|For async cleanup: IAsyncDisposable with `await using`.
p4-29.qa: IDisposable.Dispose releases unmanaged or expensive resources (connections, streams, SFTP sessions) deterministically. A using statement calls Dispose at the end of the block even on exceptions; a C# 8 using declaration disposes at the end of the enclosing scope; IAsyncDisposable with await using handles async cleanup.
i: Dispose pattern with a finalizer only when you directly own unmanaged handles; prefer SafeHandle.
Don't dispose objects you don't own (DI-injected services).
HttpClient: don't dispose per request; use IHttpClientFactory.
f: What happens if you forget Dispose?
Resources stay open until the GC finalizes them, if ever, causing leaks like connection pool exhaustion.
Dispose vs finalizer?
Dispose is deterministic and called by you; finalizers run non-deterministically on the GC thread.

p4-30.a: const: compile-time constant, implicitly static, baked into calling assemblies.|readonly: set at declaration or in the constructor, per instance.|static readonly: set once per type at runtime (good for objects like a TimeSpan or a Regex).
p4-30.qa: const is a compile-time constant, implicitly static and baked into calling assemblies; readonly is set at declaration or in the constructor, per instance; static readonly is set once per type at runtime, for values like objects or computed values that can't be const.
i: Changing a public const requires recompiling consumers; prefer static readonly for public values that might change.
readonly on a reference prevents reassignment, not mutation of the object.
readonly struct and readonly members prevent defensive copies.
Example: public const int MaxRows = 10000 in a library; changing it to 20000 doesn't affect already-compiled consumers until rebuilt.
f: Can const be a DateTime?
No, only primitive types, strings and enums (or null).
Is a readonly List immutable?
No, you can still add items; use ImmutableList or IReadOnlyList.

p4-31.a: ref: pass by reference; must be initialised; the callee may change it.|out: the callee must assign it; used for TryParse-style methods.|in: read-only reference that avoids copying large structs.
p4-31.qa: ref passes a variable by reference (must be initialised; callee may change it); out requires the callee to assign it (TryParse pattern); in passes by read-only reference, avoiding copies of large structs. C# 12 added ref readonly parameters.
i: Not allowed in async methods or iterators (ref locals limited; C# 13 relaxed some rules).
ref returns and ref locals for high-performance code.
Prefer returning tuples or records for multiple results in normal code.
ref struct types (like Span<T>) can only live on the stack, which is why they can't be used in async methods.
f: Why use in?
To avoid copying large structs without allowing changes.
out vs returning a tuple?
out fits the Try pattern; tuples are often clearer otherwise.

p4-32.a: A C# 8 feature: reference types are non-nullable by default and `string?` marks a nullable one; the compiler warns on possible null dereferences.|It catches NullReferenceException bugs at compile time; we enable it in new projects.
p4-32.qa: Nullable reference types (C# 8) make reference types non-nullable by default; string? marks a nullable one, and the compiler warns on possible null dereferences or assigning null. It catches NullReferenceExceptions at compile time; it's enabled by default in new projects.
i: It's compile-time analysis only; runtime can still have nulls (deserialization, reflection).
Attributes like [NotNullWhen(true)], [MaybeNull] help the analysis.
The null-forgiving operator ! silences warnings; use sparingly.
Turn warnings into errors (Nullable enable plus TreatWarningsAsErrors) for new code.
f: Does it change runtime behaviour?
No, only warnings and metadata.
How do you migrate a big codebase?
File by file with #nullable enable, starting with core models.

p4-33.a: Concise testing and deconstruction of values: type patterns with `is`, switch expressions, property patterns, relational and list patterns.|Example: `var fee = s switch { { Express: true } => 20, { Weight: > 10 } => 12, _ => 5 };`
p4-33.qa: Pattern matching tests and deconstructs values concisely: type patterns with is, switch expressions, property patterns, relational and logical patterns (and, or, not) and list patterns (C# 11). It replaces long if/else chains with readable, compiler-checked logic.
i: Switch expressions warn on non-exhaustive matches.
is not null is the clearest null check.
Real use: switch expressions on ShipmentStatus to compute next allowed transitions, with the compiler warning on missing cases.
f: What is a discard?
_ matches anything without binding it.
Is pattern matching slower?
No, it compiles to efficient type checks and comparisons.

p4-34.a: Static methods in a static class whose first parameter is `this T`, callable as if they were instance methods.|LINQ is built on them; we use them for DI registration such as `services.AddSftpProviders()`.
p4-34.qa: Extension methods are static methods in a static class whose first parameter has this T, so they can be called as if they were instance methods; LINQ is built on them. We use them for things like service registration (services.AddSftpProviders()) and small helpers.
i: They can't access private members and lose to real instance methods with the same signature.
C# 14 adds extension members (extension blocks) including extension properties and static extensions.
Keep them discoverable and in clear namespaces.
f: Can you extend a sealed class?
Yes, extension methods work on any type.
What's new in C# 14?
Extension blocks that allow extension properties and static members.

p4-35.a: A named set of integer constants, such as `enum ShipmentStatus { Created, Shipped, Delivered }`; type-safe and readable.|[Flags] enums combine values bitwise; decide deliberately whether to store them as int or string in the database.
p4-35.qa: An enum is a named set of integer constants such as enum ShipmentStatus { Created, Shipped, Delivered }, type-safe and readable. [Flags] enums combine values with bitwise operations (powers of two), and HasFlag or bitwise checks test them.
i: Default underlying type is int; any int can be cast, so validate input (Enum.IsDefined).
Serialize as strings for APIs with JsonStringEnumConverter to keep contracts stable.
Store as strings or ints in the database deliberately; adding values in the middle changes numbers.
f: Why assign explicit values?
So reordering doesn't change stored or serialized values.
Enum vs smart enum class?
Classes can carry behaviour and data; enums are simple constants.

p4-36.a: Blocking on async code (`.Result`, `.Wait()`) when a SynchronizationContext (WinForms, classic ASP.NET) needs the blocked thread to run the continuation: each waits for the other forever.|ASP.NET Core has no such context, so it shows up as thread-pool starvation instead.|Fix: async all the way, and ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries.
p4-36.qa: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on a Task (.Result, .Wait()) while a SynchronizationContext (WinForms, WPF, classic ASP.NET) needs that same blocked thread to run the continuation: each waits for the other forever. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so it doesn't deadlock that way, but blocking still causes thread pool starvation.
i: Fix: async all the way; never block on async in request code.
Libraries use ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid capturing contexts.
If you must call async from sync (Main, legacy), GetAwaiter().GetResult() at the very top, knowing the risks.
Thread pool starvation symptoms: latency climbs, thread count grows slowly (about one thread per second injection beyond min).
f: Why does ASP.NET Core avoid the classic deadlock?
It has no request SynchronizationContext, so continuations run on any pool thread.
Is .Result ever fine?
After the task has completed (e.g. after WhenAll), it doesn't block.

p4-37.a: `ConfigureAwait(false)` tells await not to resume on the captured SynchronizationContext.|Useful in libraries and UI apps to avoid deadlocks and context switches; mostly unnecessary in ASP.NET Core app code.
p4-37.qa: ConfigureAwait(false) tells await not to resume on the captured SynchronizationContext or TaskScheduler, so the continuation runs on a thread pool thread. It matters in libraries and UI apps to avoid deadlocks and context-switch overhead; in ASP.NET Core app code it makes little difference because there's no context.
i: Library authors should still use it because their code may run under UI contexts.
.NET 8 added ConfigureAwaitOptions (e.g. SuppressThrowing, ForceYielding) for Task.
After ConfigureAwait(false), don't touch UI elements or context-bound state.
Rule of thumb: in app code (ASP.NET Core) skip it; in reusable libraries use ConfigureAwait(false) on every await.
f: Does ConfigureAwait(false) make code faster in ASP.NET Core?
Negligibly; it's mainly about correctness in libraries.
What does ForceYielding do?
Forces the continuation to be queued asynchronously even if the task already completed.

p4-38.a: Language Integrated Query: one syntax to query collections, databases (EF Core) and XML, using operators like Where, Select, GroupBy, Join and OrderBy.|Over IQueryable it is translated to SQL; over IEnumerable it runs in memory.
p4-38.qa: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) gives one syntax to query collections, databases (EF Core) and XML using operators such as Where, Select, GroupBy, Join and OrderBy, in method or query syntax. Over IEnumerable it runs in memory with delegates; over IQueryable it builds expression trees that providers translate, e.g. to SQL.
i: Deferred execution: queries run when enumerated (foreach, ToList, Count).
Multiple enumeration re-executes the query; materialise once if reused.
.NET 9 added CountBy, AggregateBy and Index; .NET 6 added Chunk, MinBy, MaxBy, DistinctBy.
c:
var late = await db.Shipments
    .Where(s => s.Status == ShipmentStatus.InTransit && s.ExpectedAt < now)
    .OrderBy(s => s.ExpectedAt)
    .Select(s => new { s.Id, s.SiteId, s.ExpectedAt })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
f: Query vs method syntax?
Same result; query syntax compiles to method calls and can be clearer for joins.
What does CountBy do?
Groups by a key and returns counts without creating groups (.NET 9).

p4-39.a: IEnumerable: forward-only iteration.|ICollection: adds Count, Add, Remove and Contains.|IList: adds index access and Insert.|Accept the smallest interface you need; return read-only types such as IReadOnlyList.
p4-39.qa: IEnumerable<T> gives forward-only iteration; ICollection<T> adds Count, Add, Remove and Contains; IList<T> adds index access and Insert. I accept the smallest interface a method needs and return read-only interfaces (IReadOnlyList, IReadOnlyCollection) to communicate intent.
i: IEnumerable may be lazy or infinite; Count() may enumerate everything.
IReadOnlyList<T> gives Count and indexing without mutation.
Arrays implement IList<T> but throw on Add.
Method parameters: accept IEnumerable<T> or IReadOnlyCollection<T>; return concrete or read-only interfaces based on what callers need.
f: Why return IReadOnlyList instead of List?
It prevents callers mutating internal state and documents intent.
Is IEnumerable always lazy?
No, it depends on the source; it's an abstraction, not a guarantee.

p4-40.a: First: the first match; throws if there is none. FirstOrDefault: returns default (null) instead.|Single: exactly one match; throws if none or more than one. SingleOrDefault: zero or one; throws if more than one.|Use Single for unique keys so duplicate data is caught.
p4-40.qa: First returns the first match and throws if none; FirstOrDefault returns default (null) instead. Single requires exactly one match and throws if none or more than one; SingleOrDefault returns default if none but still throws if more than one.
i: Use Single when duplicates indicate a data bug; First when order matters (with OrderBy).
In SQL, First becomes TOP(1); Single becomes TOP(2) to detect duplicates.
.NET 6 added FirstOrDefault(defaultValue) overloads.
FindAsync by key checks the change tracker first.
f: Which is faster in EF Core?
First (TOP 1) reads less than Single (TOP 2), but pick by meaning.
FirstOrDefault on value types?
Returns default (0 for int), which may be ambiguous.

p4-41.a: Any() stops at the first match (EXISTS in SQL); Count() counts every row.|Use Any() to check existence; the Count property on a collection is already O(1).
p4-41.qa: Any() stops at the first match and translates to EXISTS in SQL; Count() counts every matching row. Use Any() to check existence; on in-memory collections the Count property is already O(1), and LINQ Count() uses it when available.
i: Any() on IEnumerable without a predicate can use TryGetNonEnumeratedCount-like optimisations.
Count() > 0 is a common code smell (CA1827 analyzer).
In memory, LINQ Count() checks for ICollection<T> and uses .Count without enumerating.
For IQueryable, Count() becomes SELECT COUNT(*), which scans more rows than EXISTS.
f: What does EF Core generate for Any()?
SELECT CASE WHEN EXISTS (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END.
When use Count?
When you actually need the number.

p4-42.a: A lambda that captures variables from its outer scope; the compiler stores them in a hidden class so they live as long as the lambda.|Pitfalls: capturing a loop variable by mistake, or a large object that then cannot be collected.
p4-42.qa: A closure is a lambda that captures variables from its outer scope; the compiler moves them into a hidden class so they live as long as the lambda. Pitfalls include capturing a loop variable in older for loops, accidentally keeping large objects alive, and hidden allocations on hot paths.
i: foreach variables are per-iteration since C# 5; for loop variables are shared.
static lambdas (C# 9) prevent capture and allocations.
Captured variables are shared: changing them later changes what the lambda sees.
f: Do closures allocate?
Yes, a display class instance and a delegate, unless the lambda is static or captures nothing.
Why can closures cause memory leaks?
Long-lived delegates (event handlers) keep captured objects alive.

p4-43.a: Subtypes must work wherever the base type is expected, without changing correct behaviour.|Good: every ISftpClient provider honours the same contract, for example throwing SftpTransferException on failure and never failing silently.|Violation: a ReadOnlyRepository that throws NotSupportedException on Save; split the interface instead.
p4-43.qa: Liskov Substitution says subtypes must work anywhere the base type is expected without breaking correct behaviour. Every ISftpClient provider honours the same contract (same exceptions, same semantics for overwrite), so callers never special-case one; the classic violation is Square inheriting Rectangle and breaking width/height expectations.
i: Violations: throwing NotSupportedException in overrides, stronger preconditions, weaker postconditions.
ReadOnlyCollection implementing IList and throwing on Add is a known framework compromise.
Contract tests run the same test suite against every implementation.
Our provider contract tests ran the same suite (upload, list, overwrite, error mapping) against Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, enforcing LSP.
f: How do you test LSP?
Shared contract tests for all implementations of an interface.
What smell suggests an LSP break?
Callers checking concrete types with is or casts.

p4-44.a: Clients should not depend on methods they do not use.|Example: IShipmentReader for queries and IShipmentWriter for commands instead of one large IShipmentRepository, so a reporting service only gets read access and tests mock less.
p4-44.qa: Interface Segregation says clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Instead of one large IShipmentRepository, we use IShipmentReader for queries and IShipmentWriter for commands, so a reporting service only gets read access and tests mock less.
i: Small, role-based interfaces; one class can implement several.
Fits CQRS read/write split.
Fat interfaces force empty implementations and change ripple.
Microsoft's own example: IReadOnlyList<T> separated from IList<T> for consumers that only read.
f: Doesn't this create too many interfaces?
Only split where clients really differ.
Link to security?
Read-only interfaces make accidental writes impossible in reporting code.

p4-45.a: High-level modules depend on abstractions, not on concrete classes.|Example: VendorExchangeService depends on ISftpClient injected through ASP.NET Core DI; the Rebex implementation is registered in Program.cs, so business code never references Rebex.
p4-45.qa: Dependency Inversion says high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete classes, and abstractions are owned by the high-level side. VendorExchangeService depends on ISftpClient injected through ASP.NET Core DI, not on Rebex directly, so libraries can change without touching business logic.
i: DIP is the principle; DI is the technique; IoC containers are tooling.
Clean Architecture: interfaces in the domain/application layer, implementations in infrastructure.
Without DIP: VendorExchangeService news up RebexClient directly, so changing libraries means editing business code.
With DIP: the service owns the ISftpClient abstraction and infrastructure implements it.
f: DIP vs DI?
DIP is the design principle; DI is how dependencies are supplied.
Where should the interface live?
With the code that uses it, not with the implementation.

p4-46.a: To decouple callers from implementations (three SFTP libraries), enable DI and unit testing with Moq, and add providers without changing callers (open/closed).|A base class carries the shared code; the interface is the contract.
p4-46.qa: I chose an interface to decouple callers from three SFTP implementations, enable DI and unit tests with Moq, and add providers without changing callers (open/closed). It also lets me map library-specific behaviour to one consistent contract.
i: Interfaces for seams: external systems, I/O, time (TimeProvider), randomness.
Don't create interfaces for every class "just because"; one implementation and no test need is a smell.
Interfaces also let you add decorators (logging, retry, metrics) around an implementation without changing it.
Consider an abstract base class when implementations share most code; we used both.
f: Interface vs abstract class here?
Interface for the contract plus an abstract base class for shared retry/logging.
How did it help testing?
Callers are tested with mocked ISftpClient, no real server needed.

p4-47.a: When the relationship is not truly is-a, when behaviour varies independently (use strategy or composition), when hierarchies get deep, or across module boundaries where a base change breaks many children.
p4-47.qa: I avoid inheritance when the relationship isn't truly is-a, when behaviour varies independently (use strategy or composition), when hierarchies get deep, or across module boundaries where base changes ripple. Composition over inheritance keeps classes flexible.
i: Decorator pattern adds behaviour without subclassing (e.g. a logging ISftpClient wrapper).
Sealing classes by default prevents accidental hierarchies.
Example: a RetryingSftpClient decorator wraps any ISftpClient instead of a RetryingRebexClient subclass per library.
Inheritance across assemblies couples release cycles: a base class change can break consumers.
f: Example of composition in your code?
Providers receive a retry policy and logger rather than inheriting them in newer code.
When is inheritance right?
Stable is-a relationships with shared behaviour, like framework base classes (ControllerBase).

p4-48.a: Collections pause threads (briefly for Gen 0, longer for Gen 2), and high allocation rates trigger more collections, which raises p99 latency.|Reduce allocations: pooling (ArrayPool), Span<T>, no boxing, avoid large temporary strings and LOH objects; Server GC for throughput; measure with dotnet-counters.
p4-48.qa: Garbage collections pause threads (briefly for Gen 0/1, longer for Gen 2 and LOH compaction) and high allocation rates trigger more collections, raising p99 latency and CPU. I reduce allocations on hot paths (pooling, Span, avoiding LINQ in tight loops, streaming), and measure with dotnet-counters and profilers.
i: Generational GC: Gen 0 (short-lived), Gen 1, Gen 2 (long-lived), LOH and POH.
Server GC for throughput (one heap per core); DATAS (default for Server GC since .NET 9) adapts heap count to reduce memory.
Background GC lets Gen 2 run concurrently.
ArrayPool<T>, RecyclableMemoryStream, object pooling for big buffers.
f: What is the POH?
Pinned Object Heap (.NET 5+) for objects that must not move, reducing fragmentation.
Should you call GC.Collect?
Almost never; it usually hurts performance.

p4-49.a: The exception is captured in the returned Task and rethrown at the await, with its stack trace.|If the Task is never awaited the exception is unobserved and lost; in `async void` it crashes the process.|With Task.WhenAll, await throws the first exception, and the task's Exception holds all of them.
p4-49.qa: An exception in an async method is captured in the returned Task and rethrown at the await with its stack trace. If the Task is never awaited, the exception is unobserved (TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException) and silently lost; async void exceptions crash the process because there's no Task to hold them.
i: Await every task; avoid fire-and-forget without handling.
Task.WhenAll throws the first exception at await; inspect task.Exception for all.
async void only for event handlers.
Background work: BackgroundService or a queue with try/catch and logging.
f: How do you get all exceptions from WhenAll?
Keep the WhenAll task and read its Exception.InnerExceptions.
Do exceptions thrown before the first await behave differently?
They're still captured in the Task for async methods.

p4-50.a: A technique where an object receives its dependencies from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself.|Why: loose coupling, testability (inject mocks), swapping implementations by configuration, and central lifetime management.
p4-50.qa: Dependency injection means an object receives its dependencies from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them. It gives loose coupling, easy testing with mocks, central lifetime management and configuration, and ASP.NET Core has a built-in container.
i: Lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped (per request), Transient.
Keyed services (.NET 8) for multiple named implementations.
ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild in Development catch lifetime and registration errors early.
c:
builder.Services.AddScoped<IShipmentService, ShipmentService>();
public class ShipmentsController(IShipmentService svc) : ControllerBase { }  // primary constructor
f: Is DI only for testing?
No, it also centralises configuration and lifetimes and decouples modules.
When would you use a third-party container?
For features like decorators, interception or assembly scanning (Autofac, Scrutor for scanning).

p4-51.a: Any object a class needs to do its work, such as a repository, an HttpClient, a logger or an ISftpClient.
p4-51.qa: A dependency is any object a class needs to do its work, such as a repository, an HttpClient, a logger, configuration, a clock (TimeProvider) or an ISftpClient.
i: Hidden dependencies: static calls (DateTime.Now, File.ReadAllText) make code hard to test.
Make them explicit through constructor parameters.
Dependencies can be services, configuration (IOptions<T>), time (TimeProvider), randomness and the file system.
The fewer and more abstract the dependencies, the easier the class is to test and change.
f: Is DateTime.Now a dependency?
Yes, a hidden one; inject TimeProvider.
What are too many dependencies a sign of?
The class likely has too many responsibilities.

p4-52.a: Inversion of Control: the framework, not your code, controls object creation and flow (don't call us, we'll call you); DI is one form of it.|An IoC container (the built-in ServiceCollection/ServiceProvider, Autofac) registers types, builds object graphs and manages lifetimes and disposal.
p4-52.qa: Inversion of Control means the framework, not your code, controls object creation and flow ("don't call us, we'll call you"); DI is one form. An IoC container registers services and lifetimes and builds object graphs automatically; ASP.NET Core's is Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.
i: Other IoC forms: events, template methods, middleware pipelines.
Container builds graphs recursively by constructor parameters.
ASP.NET Core itself is IoC: it calls your middleware, controllers and hosted services; you don't call them.
Containers also manage lifetimes and disposal, not just construction.
f: Does the built-in container support property injection?
No, only constructor injection (plus [FromServices] and [FromKeyedServices] in endpoints).
What is ActivatorUtilities?
A helper to create objects mixing container services and explicit arguments.

p4-53.a: Constructor: dependencies are required, immutable and explicit; the default in ASP.NET Core.|Property: optional dependencies set after construction; the built-in container does not support it (Autofac does).|Too many constructor parameters means the class does too much.
p4-53.qa: Constructor injection makes dependencies required, immutable and explicit, and it's the default in ASP.NET Core; property injection sets optional dependencies after construction and is not supported by the built-in container. Method injection ([FromServices] on an action parameter) suits rarely used dependencies.
i: Primary constructors (C# 12) reduce boilerplate; parameters are captured, not readonly fields, so assign to readonly fields if immutability matters.
Too many constructor parameters signals a class doing too much.
Property injection hides required dependencies and allows half-initialised objects.
Method injection in minimal APIs: handler parameters are resolved from DI per request.
f: Why prefer constructor injection?
Objects are always valid after construction and dependencies are visible.
Are primary constructor parameters readonly?
No, they're mutable captured parameters unless assigned to readonly fields.

p4-54.a: The built container that resolves services (GetService), created from IServiceCollection when the host is built.|Scopes come from IServiceScopeFactory; HttpContext.RequestServices is the current request's scope.
p4-54.qa: IServiceProvider is the built container that resolves services (GetService), created from IServiceCollection when the host is built. Scopes come from IServiceScopeFactory, and each request has its own scoped provider in HttpContext.RequestServices.
i: Root provider resolving scoped services is a bug (caught by ValidateScopes in Development).
IServiceProviderIsService checks registration without resolving.
Keyed lookup: GetRequiredKeyedService<T>(key).
Building the provider: builder.Build() creates the root provider; Development validates scopes and the graph when ValidateOnBuild is on.
f: Why not resolve scoped services from the root?
They'd live for the app's lifetime, becoming captive.
What is RequestServices?
The request-scoped provider used to create controllers and middleware dependencies.

p4-55.a: Rule: a service may depend on services that live at least as long as it does.|Singleton on Transient: allowed, but the transient effectively becomes a singleton. Singleton on Scoped: not allowed (captive dependency; scope validation throws in Development).|Scoped on Singleton or Transient: fine. Transient on Scoped: fine when resolved inside a scope.
p4-55.qa: A service may depend on services that live at least as long as it does. Singleton on Scoped is a captive dependency bug (DbContext held forever, shared across threads); Singleton on Transient is allowed but the transient effectively becomes a singleton; Scoped on Singleton and Transient on anything are fine.
i: ValidateScopes (on in Development) throws for singleton-to-scoped.
Fix singletons needing scoped services: IServiceScopeFactory, create a scope per unit of work.
IDbContextFactory for singletons or background work needing DbContext.
Example captive bug: a singleton cache holding a scoped DbContext ends up sharing one context across threads and requests.
f: What is a captive dependency?
A shorter-lived service captured by a longer-lived one.
How do you catch it before production?
ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild, plus tests that build the host.

p4-56.a: GetService returns null if the service is not registered; GetRequiredService throws InvalidOperationException.|Prefer GetRequiredService to fail fast, and prefer constructor injection over both.
p4-56.qa: GetService returns null if the service isn't registered; GetRequiredService throws InvalidOperationException. I prefer GetRequiredService to fail fast with a clear message, and use GetService only for truly optional services.
i: Both are service locator calls; prefer constructor injection.
IEnumerable<T> resolves to empty if none registered, never null.
GetRequiredService gives a clear error naming the missing type, much easier to debug than a NullReferenceException later.
Keyed versions: GetKeyedService / GetRequiredKeyedService.
f: When use GetService?
Optional plugins or features that may not be registered.
Is GetRequiredService an extension method?
Yes, in ServiceProviderServiceExtensions.

p4-57.a: Controllers declare dependencies in their constructor. For each request the controller activator creates the controller from the request scope (HttpContext.RequestServices), resolving the whole graph recursively.|Minimal APIs inject handler parameters directly; [FromServices] works on action parameters.
p4-57.qa: Controllers declare dependencies in their constructor; for each request, the controller activator creates the controller from the request scope (HttpContext.RequestServices), so scoped services like DbContext are shared within that request and disposed when it ends. Controllers themselves aren't registered by default; AddControllersAsServices changes that.
i: Middleware constructors resolve once (singleton-like); request-scoped services go in InvokeAsync parameters.
Minimal API handlers get services as parameters, inferred from DI.
Constructor selection: the container picks the constructor with the most parameters it can satisfy.
Primary constructors (C# 12) work the same way for controllers.
f: Are controllers singletons?
No, a new instance per request.
What does AddControllersAsServices do?
Registers controllers in DI so the container (and features like decorators) creates them.

p4-58.a: Register several: `AddTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>()` and `AddTransient<INotifier, SmsNotifier>()`.|Inject `IEnumerable<INotifier>` to get all of them; a single INotifier gets the last registration.|.NET 8 keyed services: `AddKeyedScoped<ISftpClient, RebexClient>(key)` with `[FromKeyedServices(key)]`, or a factory that selects by configuration.
p4-58.qa: Register several implementations (AddTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>(), AddTransient<INotifier, SmsNotifier>()) and inject IEnumerable<INotifier> to get all; injecting INotifier gets the last registered. To pick one, use keyed services (.NET 8: AddKeyedSingleton<ISftpClient, RebexClient>("Rebex") with [FromKeyedServices]) or a factory.
i: TryAddEnumerable avoids duplicate registrations.
Keyed services fit our per-vendor SFTP provider choice from configuration.
Order matters: IEnumerable<T> preserves registration order, which can define a pipeline (e.g. validators).
f: Which one is resolved for a single INotifier?
The last registration.
Keyed services vs factory?
Keyed is built in and simple; factories allow custom logic.

p4-59.a: Yes: `using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();` then resolve from `scope.ServiceProvider`.|Use it in singletons and BackgroundServices that need scoped services such as DbContext, one scope per unit of work (for example per queue message).
p4-59.qa: Yes: using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope() and resolve from scope.ServiceProvider. I use IServiceScopeFactory in singletons and BackgroundServices that need scoped services like DbContext, creating one scope per unit of work (per message or per poll) so they're disposed properly.
i: CreateAsyncScope with await using for IAsyncDisposable services.
Never keep a scope for the whole app lifetime.
Scoped services resolved inside the scope are disposed when the scope is disposed, preventing leaks.
f: Why one scope per message?
So DbContext tracking and connections don't grow across messages.
CreateScope vs CreateAsyncScope?
The async version supports await using for async disposal.

p4-60.a: Pulling dependencies from IServiceProvider inside classes instead of declaring them in the constructor.|It hides dependencies, makes tests harder and fails at runtime; acceptable only in composition roots, factories and middleware.
p4-60.qa: Service locator is pulling dependencies from IServiceProvider inside classes instead of declaring them in the constructor. It hides dependencies, makes tests harder and moves errors to runtime. It's acceptable at composition roots, factories and background scopes.
i: Smell: IServiceProvider in a business class constructor.
Testing requires a container or complex mocks.
Legitimate uses: factory classes, middleware InvokeAsync parameters are fine; static service locators (ServiceLocator.Current) are not.
Detect it in reviews: IServiceProvider injected into domain classes.
f: Is using IServiceScopeFactory a service locator?
Technically yes, but it's an accepted infrastructure exception.
How do you refactor away from it?
Move dependencies to constructor parameters or inject a typed factory.

p4-61.a: Do not use the container: construct the class directly with Moq mocks for its interfaces, call the method, and assert outcomes and key interactions.|Test the wiring separately by building the ServiceProvider with ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes.
p4-61.qa: I don't use the container in unit tests: I construct the class directly with Moq mocks (or fakes) for its interfaces, call the method, and assert outcomes and key interactions. For wiring, I use integration tests with WebApplicationFactory and replace external services with ConfigureTestServices.
i: Prefer state-based assertions over verifying every call.
FakeTimeProvider, FakeLogger from Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing.
Integration example: WebApplicationFactory with ConfigureTestServices to replace ISftpClient with a fake.
f: Unit vs integration test?
Unit isolates one class; integration tests real wiring, often with a real database in containers.
What is Testcontainers?
A library that starts real dependencies (SQL Server, RabbitMQ) in Docker for tests.

p4-62.a: VendorExchangeService receives ISftpClientFactory, IOptions<SftpOptions> and ILogger through its constructor; the factory returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro provider from configuration.|DbContext is Scoped, the RabbitMQ connection is a Singleton, validators are Transient.
p4-62.qa: VendorExchangeService receives ISftpClientFactory, IOptions<SftpOptions> and ILogger<T> through its constructor; the factory returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro client per vendor configuration. It's scoped, the factory is a singleton, and clients are created and disposed per transfer.
i: Registration via an AddSftpProviders extension method.
Options validated at startup.
Unit tests mock the factory and client.
Registration with keyed services: AddKeyedTransient<ISftpClient, RebexSftpClient>("Rebex"), resolved by vendor configuration.
f: Why is the factory a singleton?
It's stateless and cheap to share.
Why create clients per transfer?
SFTP sessions are stateful connections that should be disposed after use.

p4-63.a: Singleton: shared across threads and requests, so any state must be thread-safe, and holding scoped resources like DbContext causes captive-dependency bugs and stale data.|Transient everywhere: needless allocations, many instances of expensive objects, and no per-request sharing such as one unit of work.
p4-63.qa: Singletons are shared across threads and requests, so any state must be thread-safe, and holding scoped resources like DbContext causes captive dependency bugs. Everything transient creates many short-lived objects (GC pressure) and breaks sharing within a request, such as one DbContext per unit of work.
i: Choose by state: stateless and thread-safe → singleton; per-request state → scoped; lightweight, stateful per use → transient.
HttpClient handlers are pooled by IHttpClientFactory, not singleton HttpClients with stale DNS.
Transient disposables resolved from the root container are tracked until shutdown, effectively a memory leak.
Rule: singleton for stateless/thread-safe, scoped for per-request state, transient for lightweight stateless helpers.
f: Is DbContext thread-safe?
No, which is why it's scoped and never shared across concurrent operations.
Should a cache be singleton?
Yes, with thread-safe structures like IMemoryCache.

p4-64.a: The request's DI scope is disposed: every Scoped and Transient IDisposable created in it is disposed (DbContext closes its connection), and the HttpContext is returned for reuse.
p4-64.qa: When a request ends, its DI scope is disposed: every scoped and transient IDisposable created in it is disposed (DbContext closes its connection back to the pool), the HttpContext is returned for reuse, and response completion callbacks (OnCompleted) run.
i: Don't use HttpContext or scoped services after the request ends (e.g. in fire-and-forget tasks).
IHttpContextAccessor in background threads returns null or stale data.
The request's CancellationToken (RequestAborted) is signalled if the client disconnects earlier.
Scoped IAsyncDisposable services are disposed asynchronously.
f: What if you start a background task using DbContext from the request?
It may be disposed mid-use; create a new scope instead.
What is Response.OnCompleted?
A callback that runs after the response is sent, useful for metrics.

p4-65.a: The container disposes what it created: scoped and transient disposables when their scope ends, singletons when the root provider is disposed at shutdown.|Instances you create yourself and register (`AddSingleton(new X())`) are not disposed by the container.|Avoid resolving transient disposables from the root provider: they live until shutdown, which is a leak.
p4-65.qa: The container disposes what it created: scoped and transient disposables when their scope ends, singletons when the root provider is disposed at shutdown. Instances you create yourself and register (AddSingleton(new X())) are not disposed by the container.
i: Transient disposables resolved from the root live until shutdown, a memory leak pattern.
IAsyncDisposable is supported; prefer async disposal at shutdown.
Factories like AddSingleton(sp => new X()) are disposed by the container because it created them via the factory.
IDisposable transients resolved repeatedly from the root are a classic leak; use scopes.
f: Why are transient disposables from the root a leak?
The root tracks them for disposal, so they stay referenced until the app stops.
Who disposes a singleton you constructed?
You do; the container won't.

p4-66.a: Microsoft's cross-platform, open-source, high-performance framework for web APIs, MVC and real-time apps on modern .NET, with built-in DI, configuration, logging and the Kestrel server.
p4-66.qa: ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's cross-platform, open-source, high-performance framework for web APIs, MVC, Razor Pages, Blazor and real-time apps (SignalR) on modern .NET, with built-in DI, configuration, logging, a middleware pipeline and the Kestrel server. It runs on Windows, Linux and containers.
i: Hosting: WebApplication builder (minimal hosting) since .NET 6.
Endpoints: controllers, minimal APIs, gRPC, SignalR hubs, health checks.
Performance features: Kestrel, System.Text.Json source generators, output caching, native AOT for minimal APIs.
.NET 10 additions: built-in validation for minimal APIs, OpenAPI 3.1 support, passkey support in Identity.
f: ASP.NET vs ASP.NET Core?
Classic ASP.NET runs only on .NET Framework/IIS; Core is a cross-platform rewrite.
Can ASP.NET Core run without IIS?
Yes, Kestrel serves directly or behind any reverse proxy.

p4-67.a: The cross-platform, async web server built into ASP.NET Core.|It runs on its own in containers or behind a reverse proxy or load balancer (ALB, IIS, Nginx) that handles TLS and extras.
p4-67.qa: Kestrel is the cross-platform, async web server built into ASP.NET Core. It can serve traffic directly or sit behind a reverse proxy or load balancer (ALB, Nginx, IIS via the ASP.NET Core Module) that handles TLS termination, buffering and edge concerns.
i: Supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC).
Configurable limits: MaxRequestBodySize (default about 30 MB), header sizes, connection limits, timeouts.
Behind proxies, use ForwardedHeaders middleware to get the real client IP and scheme.
IIS in-process hosting runs the app inside w3wp without Kestrel.
f: Why use a reverse proxy?
TLS offload, load balancing, WAF and centralised edge security.
What header does ForwardedHeaders read?
X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, from trusted proxies only.

p4-68.a: Things break quietly: UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication leaves the user anonymous (401/403); UseCors after the endpoints means no CORS headers; a late exception handler misses earlier errors; static files after auth forces auth on them.
p4-68.qa: Middleware order is execution order, so mistakes break things quietly: UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication leaves users anonymous (401/403), UseCors after endpoints means no CORS headers, exception handling registered late misses earlier errors, and static files after auth either get protected unintentionally or bypass checks.
i: Recommended order: ExceptionHandler, HSTS, HttpsRedirection, StaticFiles, Routing, CORS, Authentication, Authorization, RateLimiter, custom, endpoints.
WebApplication adds UseRouting and endpoints automatically if you don't.
Part 10 Q1 has the full pipeline diagram.
Real example: putting app.UseCors() after app.MapControllers() means preflight responses miss headers and the browser blocks calls.
f: What happens if UseRateLimiter is before UseRouting?
Endpoint-specific policies can't be read; only global limiters apply.
Where does correlation-id middleware go?
Very early, so all later logs include it.

p4-69.a: Use: adds middleware that can call next.|Run: terminal middleware that ends the pipeline.|Map / MapWhen: branch the pipeline by path or condition.
p4-69.qa: Use adds middleware that can do work and call next; Run adds terminal middleware that ends the pipeline; Map branches by path prefix and MapWhen by a predicate into a separate pipeline; UseWhen conditionally adds middleware and then rejoins the main pipeline.
i: Map strips the matched prefix from Request.Path and adds it to PathBase.
Prefer endpoint routing (MapGet, MapControllers) for routes; Map is for pipeline branches.
Map with nested pipelines can host separate branches, e.g. /admin with its own auth middleware.
c:
app.UseWhen(ctx => ctx.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/api"), a => a.UseMiddleware<AuditMiddleware>());
app.Map("/ping", a => a.Run(ctx => ctx.Response.WriteAsync("pong")));
f: MapWhen vs UseWhen?
MapWhen branches without rejoining; UseWhen rejoins the main pipeline.
What happens after Run?
Nothing; later middleware never executes.

p4-70.a: UseRouting matches the request to an endpoint early and stores it on HttpContext; middleware in between (CORS, auth) can read endpoint metadata such as [Authorize]; the endpoint runs at the end.|One routing system for controllers, minimal APIs, gRPC and health checks.
p4-70.qa: With endpoint routing, UseRouting matches the request to an endpoint early and stores it on HttpContext, so middleware in between (CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting) can read endpoint metadata like [Authorize] or policies; UseEndpoints (or the implicit endpoint middleware) then executes it.
i: ctx.GetEndpoint() returns the matched endpoint and its metadata.
Route constraints ({id:int}), route groups (MapGroup) for shared prefixes and policies.
LinkGenerator generates URLs from route names.
c:
var api = app.MapGroup("/api/shipments").RequireAuthorization().WithTags("Shipments");
api.MapGet("/{id:int}", (int id, IShipmentService s) => s.GetAsync(id));
f: Why was endpoint routing introduced?
So all frameworks share one routing system and middleware can see the chosen endpoint.
What is MapGroup?
A way to apply a prefix and conventions to many endpoints.

p4-71.a: Since .NET 6 the minimal hosting model merges Startup's ConfigureServices and Configure into Program.cs (`builder.Services...`, `app.Use...`). A Startup class still works if you keep one.
p4-71.qa: Since .NET 6 the minimal hosting model merges Startup's ConfigureServices and Configure into Program.cs (builder.Services... then app.Use...). A Startup class still works if you call it yourself, but new templates don't use it.
i: WebApplication.CreateBuilder configures configuration, logging, DI and Kestrel with sensible defaults.
Top-level statements; make Program partial or public for WebApplicationFactory tests (.NET 10 generates this automatically).
Extension methods keep Program.cs tidy (AddIrtServices()).
Testing: in .NET 10 a source generator makes Program public automatically for WebApplicationFactory.
f: How do integration tests find Program?
WebApplicationFactory<Program>; Program must be accessible (public partial class Program).
Is Startup deprecated?
Not removed, but no longer the default pattern.

p4-72.a: Not as server protection: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy and does not stop curl, Postman or server-to-server calls.|Real security is authentication and authorization; CORS only controls which browser origins may read responses.
p4-72.qa: CORS doesn't protect the server: it relaxes the browser's same-origin policy and doesn't stop curl, Postman or server-to-server calls. Real security is authentication, authorization and validation; CORS only controls which browser origins can read responses.
i: Never combine AllowAnyOrigin with AllowCredentials (not allowed and unsafe).
Preflight OPTIONS requests for non-simple requests; cache with SetPreflightMaxAge.
Allow-list specific origins per environment.
f: What is a preflight?
An OPTIONS request the browser sends to ask permission for non-simple cross-origin requests.
Does CORS stop CSRF?
Not fully; simple form posts don't preflight, so use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.

p4-73.a: UseHttpsRedirection and UseHsts in production; certificates on Kestrel or, more commonly, TLS terminated at the ALB or API Gateway with ACM certificates, plus HTTPS between components where policy requires it.
p4-73.qa: In production I use UseHttpsRedirection and UseHsts, with certificates either on Kestrel or, more commonly, TLS terminated at the ALB or API Gateway with ACM certificates and ForwardedHeaders so the app knows the original scheme. Internal traffic can be re-encrypted where policy requires.
i: HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a period; don't enable it in development.
TLS 1.2+ only; modern ciphers.
Certificate rotation automated by ACM.
dotnet dev-certs for local HTTPS.
f: Why ForwardedHeaders with TLS offload?
Otherwise the app sees HTTP and may redirect loop or generate wrong URLs.
What is HSTS preload?
Browsers ship a list of HTTPS-only domains so even the first visit uses HTTPS.

p4-74.a: AddHealthChecks with checks for the database, RabbitMQ and other dependencies, exposed with MapHealthChecks (for example /health/live and /health/ready).|Load balancers, ECS and Kubernetes use them to route traffic and replace unhealthy instances.
p4-74.qa: AddHealthChecks registers checks for the database, RabbitMQ and other dependencies, exposed with MapHealthChecks, typically /health/live (process only) and /health/ready (dependencies). Load balancers and orchestrators use them to route traffic and restart unhealthy instances.
i: Tags and predicates separate live and ready checks.
AspNetCore.HealthChecks.* packages provide checks for SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, URIs.
Custom IHealthCheck for business checks (e.g. SFTP reachable).
Don't expose detailed health output publicly; secure or minimise it.
f: Should liveness check the database?
No, or a DB blip restarts every instance.
What is Degraded used for?
Partial health that alerts without removing the instance.

p4-75.a: On SIGTERM the host stops accepting requests, lets in-flight ones finish within the shutdown timeout, and signals ApplicationStopping and the BackgroundService stopping token.|Consumers stop fetching, finish and ack current messages, then close connections; ECS and Kubernetes allow a grace period before killing the process.
p4-75.qa: On SIGTERM the host stops accepting new requests, lets in-flight ones finish within the shutdown timeout (30 seconds by default since .NET 6; previously 5 seconds), signals ApplicationStopping and cancels BackgroundService tokens, then disposes services. Orchestrators must allow enough time (ECS stopTimeout, Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds) and load balancers should deregister first.
i: HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout configures the wait.
Background workers: stop taking new messages, finish or nack the current one.
ALB deregistration delay should be shorter than the stop timeout.
f: What happens if shutdown exceeds the timeout?
The orchestrator sends SIGKILL and work in progress is lost.
How do message consumers shut down safely?
Stop consuming, finish current messages and ack, or let unacked ones redeliver.

p4-76.a: Accept a CancellationToken in actions (bound to HttpContext.RequestAborted) and pass it to EF Core, HttpClient and delays, so abandoned requests stop working.|Combine with timeouts via CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter and handle OperationCanceledException quietly.
p4-76.qa: I accept a CancellationToken in actions (bound to HttpContext.RequestAborted) and pass it through to EF Core, HttpClient, Task.Delay and other async calls, so abandoned requests stop work; in workers I use the stoppingToken. I check ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() in long loops and treat OperationCanceledException as normal, not an error.
i: Don't cancel after a point of no return (e.g. after committing); pass CancellationToken.None to cleanup.
CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource combines tokens; CancelAfter adds timeouts.
Log cancellations at lower levels to avoid noise.
f: What happens when a client disconnects?
RequestAborted is signalled, and awaiting cancellable calls throws OperationCanceledException.
Should writes be cancellable?
Be careful; partial work must be transactional or idempotent.

p4-77.a: PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent; missing fields become defaults.|PATCH applies a partial change (JSON Patch or merge patch); use it to update a few fields.
p4-77.qa: PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent, so missing fields become defaults; PATCH applies a partial change (JSON Patch or JSON Merge Patch) and isn't guaranteed idempotent. I use PATCH for small updates like status changes and PUT when the client sends the full representation.
i: JSON Patch (RFC 6902): operations list; JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396): partial document.
.NET 10 adds JSON Patch support on System.Text.Json (previously required Newtonsoft).
Use ETags/If-Match for concurrency on both.
PATCH with JSON Merge Patch: send only changed fields; null means remove.
f: Can PUT create resources?
Yes, if the client chooses the id (PUT /items/42).
Is PATCH idempotent?
Can be, but not by definition (e.g. "add item" operations).

p4-78.a: 200 OK: success with a body.|201 Created: a new resource was created; return a Location header and usually the resource.
p4-78.qa: 200 OK means success with a body; 201 Created means a new resource was created, with a Location header pointing to it and usually the resource in the body. Others in the family: 202 Accepted (processing later) and 204 No Content (success without body).
i: CreatedAtAction / Results.Created set Location.
202 with a status URL suits long jobs like CSV import.
201 vs 202: 201 means created now; 202 means accepted for later processing.
c: return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = shipment.Id }, dto);
f: When 202?
When work is queued and finishes later.
204 vs 200 with empty body?
204 explicitly says no content; common for DELETE and PUT.

p4-79.a: 400 Bad Request: invalid input.|401 Unauthorized: not authenticated (missing or invalid token).|403 Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed.
p4-79.qa: 400 Bad Request means invalid input; 401 Unauthorized means not authenticated (missing or invalid token, with a WWW-Authenticate header); 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed.
i: Return ProblemDetails with validation errors for 400.
For resources the user may not know exist, 404 can hide existence instead of 403.
ASP.NET Core returns 401 via the authentication handler's challenge and 403 via forbid.
Return ProblemDetails consistently for all three.
f: Which code for an expired token?
What does WWW-Authenticate tell the client?
The scheme and error, e.g. Bearer error="invalid_token".

p4-80.a: 404 Not Found: the resource or route does not exist.|405 Method Not Allowed: the route exists but not for this verb, for example DELETE on a read-only endpoint.
p4-80.qa: 404 Not Found means the resource or route doesn't exist; 405 Method Not Allowed means the route exists but not for this HTTP verb (e.g. DELETE on a read-only endpoint), and the response should include an Allow header.
i: Endpoint routing returns 405 automatically when a route matches but the method doesn't.
Return 404 for missing ids, not 200 with null.
In ASP.NET Core, endpoint routing returns 405 when a route matches but no endpoint supports the method.
Use 404 for "no such resource id" rather than 200 with null.
f: 410 Gone means it existed and was permanently removed.
Why would you get 405 unexpectedly?
Missing [HttpPut] or a WebDAV module in IIS intercepting verbs.

p4-81.a: 409 Conflict: a valid request clashes with the current state (duplicate, concurrency version mismatch).|422 Unprocessable Entity: well-formed but semantically invalid (business validation fails).
p4-81.qa: 409 Conflict means a valid request clashes with current state (duplicate, concurrency version mismatch); 422 Unprocessable Content means the request is well-formed but semantically invalid (business rule failed). Many APIs use 400 for validation; I use 422 for business rule failures when the team agrees.
i: 412 Precondition Failed for If-Match ETag mismatch.
Be consistent and document the choices.
409 example: inserting a site number that already exists in the study.
422 example: kit count exceeds depot stock, a valid request breaking a business rule.
f: Which for a duplicate import file?
409, with the existing import id.
Which for a concurrency conflict in EF Core?
409 (or 412 with ETags).

p4-82.a: 500: unhandled error in this server.|502 Bad Gateway: a proxy or gateway got an invalid response from upstream.|503 Service Unavailable: overloaded or down (maintenance, no healthy targets); send Retry-After. 504 is an upstream timeout.
p4-82.qa: 500 is an unhandled error in this server; 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or gateway got an invalid response from upstream; 503 Service Unavailable means overloaded or down for maintenance (often with Retry-After); 504 means the gateway timed out waiting for upstream.
i: ALB 502 often means the target closed the connection or returned malformed responses (keep-alive timeout mismatches).
ALB 504 means the target didn't respond within the idle timeout.
429 Too Many Requests for rate limiting.
503 should include Retry-After when planned maintenance or overload.
f: Why might ALB return 502 intermittently?
Target keep-alive timeout shorter than ALB idle timeout, so connections close unexpectedly.
What does 503 from ALB mean?
No healthy targets registered.

p4-83.a: Data Transfer Objects: simple classes or records that shape exactly what an API accepts or returns.|Why: decouple the API contract from the DB schema, hide internal and sensitive fields, prevent over-posting, validate inputs and version independently.
p4-83.qa: DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) are simple classes or records that shape exactly what an API accepts or returns. They decouple the API contract from the database schema, prevent over-posting and data leaks, allow versioning, and let each endpoint carry only what it needs.
i: Records are ideal: immutable, value equality, concise.
Map with explicit code, Mapperly (source generated) or AutoMapper (now commercial for new versions).
Separate request and response DTOs.
c:
public sealed record CreateShipmentRequest(int SiteId, int KitCount, DateOnly ShipDate);
public sealed record ShipmentResponse(int Id, string Status, DateTimeOffset? DeliveredAt);
f: AutoMapper or manual mapping?
Manual or source-generated mapping is explicit and fast; AutoMapper hides errors until runtime.
Should DTOs have logic?
No, only data and validation attributes.

p4-84.a: It leaks the schema and sensitive fields, couples clients to DB changes, enables over-posting, and causes serialization cycles and lazy-loading surprises.|Map to DTOs with Select projections, Mapster or AutoMapper.
p4-84.qa: Exposing EF entities directly leaks the schema and sensitive fields, couples clients to database changes, enables over-posting, and causes serialization cycles and lazy-loading surprises. DTOs give a stable, safe contract.
i: Navigation properties create cycles (JSON ReferenceHandler is a band-aid).
Lazy loading during serialization creates N+1 queries.
Projection with Select into DTOs also generates efficient SQL.
Security example: an entity with IsUnblinded or audit fields accidentally serialized to the client.
f: How do you return data efficiently?
Project to DTOs in the query so only needed columns are selected.
What is over-posting?
Clients setting fields they shouldn't by sending extra properties.

p4-85.a: DTO: the transport shape between layers or services (API contracts).|ViewModel: shaped for one UI view and may include display-only data. In APIs we mostly talk about DTOs.
p4-85.qa: A DTO is the transport shape between layers or services (API contracts); a ViewModel is shaped for one UI view and may include display-only data like dropdown options. In APIs we mostly use DTOs; ViewModels belong to MVC or front-end code.
i: BFF responses are close to view models for a specific screen.
Keep both free of business logic.
In our APIs, request DTOs (commands) and response DTOs (views) are separate records.
ViewModels belong to Razor/MVC; in React the client shapes its own view state.
f: Can a DTO be a ViewModel?
Sometimes, if the API is designed for one screen.
What is a command object?
An input DTO that represents an intent, as in CQRS.

p4-86.a: An attribute that turns on API behaviours: attribute routing is required, invalid model state returns 400 ProblemDetails automatically, binding sources are inferred ([FromBody] for complex types), and errors use ProblemDetails.
p4-86.qa: [ApiController] turns on API behaviours: attribute routing is required, invalid model state returns 400 ProblemDetails automatically, binding sources are inferred ([FromBody] for complex types, [FromRoute]/[FromQuery] for simple ones), multipart/form-data is inferred for IFormFile, and error status codes get ProblemDetails.
i: Can be applied at assembly level.
Customise the automatic 400 with InvalidModelStateResponseFactory or disable with SuppressModelStateInvalidFilter.
Services are inferred for parameters registered in DI (.NET 7+).
Since .NET 7, parameters registered in DI are inferred as services in [ApiController] actions without [FromServices].
f: Why do some actions not hit my breakpoint with bad input?
The automatic 400 filter returns before the action runs.
How do you customise the 400 response?
Configure ApiBehaviorOptions.InvalidModelStateResponseFactory.

p4-87.a: Routing maps URLs to endpoints.|Attribute routing: `[Route(api/studies/{id})]` on controllers and actions; the standard for APIs.|Conventional routing: one template in Program.cs such as `{controller}/{action}/{id?}`; common for MVC sites.
p4-87.qa: Routing maps URLs to endpoints. Attribute routing puts templates on controllers and actions ([Route("api/studies/{id}")]) and is the standard for APIs; conventional routing uses one template in Program.cs such as {controller}/{action}/{id?}, typical for MVC sites.
i: Route constraints ({id:int}, {date:datetime}) and tokens ([controller]).
Minimal APIs use MapGet/MapPost with the same routing engine.
Avoid ambiguous routes; route order and specificity resolve matches.
Route templates support optional parameters ({id?}), defaults and catch-all ({*path}).
f: What's a route constraint for?
Matching only valid formats; not for input validation.
Can you mix both?
Yes, but APIs usually stick to attribute routing.

p4-88.a: Query parameters such as `?status=Shipped&siteId=12&sortBy=shipDate&desc=true`.|Apply them to IQueryable before paging so SQL does the work; allow-list sortable and filterable fields to prevent injection and unindexed sorts; return the total count with the page.
p4-88.qa: I accept query parameters such as ?status=Shipped&siteId=12&sortBy=shipDate&desc=true, apply them to IQueryable before paging so SQL does the work, and allow-list sortable and filterable fields to prevent injection and slow queries.
i: Build queries conditionally; never concatenate SQL.
Indexes to support common filters and sorts.
Stable sort with a tie-breaker (Id) for consistent paging.
f: Offset vs keyset paging?
Keyset (WHERE Id > last) is faster for deep pages; offset is simpler.
How do you stop huge page sizes?
Cap page size on the server.

p4-89.a: OpenAPI is the standard JSON/YAML description of an API; Swagger UI renders it interactively.|In .NET: Swashbuckle or the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, XML comments, examples and auth settings; the contract is shared with consumers and used to generate clients.
p4-89.qa: OpenAPI is the standard JSON/YAML description of an API; Swagger UI renders it interactively. In .NET 9+ the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi generates documents (Swashbuckle is no longer in templates), with XML comments, examples and auth settings; Scalar or Swagger UI can render it.
i: .NET 10 supports OpenAPI 3.1 and XML doc comments in generated docs.
Generate clients (NSwag, Kiota) from the spec.
Contract-first or code-first; version documents per API version.
f: Why did templates drop Swashbuckle?
Microsoft moved to a built-in, maintained OpenAPI generator.
How do you keep docs accurate?
Generate from code and test the spec in CI.

p4-90.a: HTTPS only; authentication with JWTs from OIDC/SSO; authorization policies and resource-level checks; input validation; rate limiting; restricted CORS; security headers; no secrets or PHI in logs; dependency scanning; least-privilege DB and IAM roles; audit logging.
p4-90.qa: HTTPS only; authentication with JWTs from OIDC/SSO; authorization policies and resource-level checks; input validation; rate limiting; restricted CORS; security headers; no secrets or PHI in logs; dependency scanning; and least-privilege access to data and cloud resources.
i: OWASP API Top 10 as the checklist (Part 2 Q51).
Secrets in Secrets Manager; managed identities/roles.
WAF at the edge, request size limits.
Audit logs for sensitive actions.
f: Most common API security bug?
Broken object level authorization (missing per-resource checks).
How do you test API security?
Automated authz tests, DAST scans and penetration tests.

p4-91.a: Access token: short-lived (for example [15 minutes]) and sent on every API call.|Refresh token: long-lived, stored securely and sent only to the identity provider to get new access tokens; it can be revoked server-side, which is how our logout fix works.
p4-91.qa: The access token is short-lived (e.g. [15 minutes]) and sent on every API call; the refresh token is long-lived, stored securely and sent only to the identity provider to get new access tokens, and it can be revoked. This limits exposure if an access token leaks.
i: Refresh token rotation: each use returns a new one; reuse of an old one signals theft.
Store refresh tokens server-side (BFF) or in secure HttpOnly cookies.
Our logout fix revokes refresh tokens and denylists access token jti.
Access tokens are validated locally by APIs; refresh tokens are validated only by the identity provider.
f: Why not long-lived access tokens?
They can't easily be revoked and increase damage if stolen.
Where should refresh tokens never be stored?
localStorage or anywhere JavaScript can read.

p4-92.a: Role-based: `[Authorize(Roles = StudyManager)]`; simple but coarse.|Policy-based: named policies with requirements and handlers registered in AddAuthorization, plus resource-based checks via IAuthorizationService (can this user access this study?).|Clinical systems need resource-level checks, not just roles.
p4-92.qa: Role-based authorization ([Authorize(Roles = "StudyManager")]) is simple but coarse; policy-based uses named policies with requirements and handlers registered in AddAuthorization, plus resource-based checks via IAuthorizationService for rules like "this user can access this study".
i: Requirements + handlers keep rules testable.
RequireAssertion for quick inline rules.
Resource-based: pass the resource to AuthorizeAsync.
f: How do you apply a policy?
[Authorize(Policy = "CanUnblind")] or RequireAuthorization("CanUnblind").
Fallback policy?
A default policy applied to endpoints without attributes, e.g. require authenticated users.

p4-93.qa: Over-posting is when clients send extra fields that bind to properties they shouldn't set (IsAdmin, Status). I prevent it with input DTOs containing only allowed fields and never binding entities directly; [Bind] or [BindNever] are weaker alternatives.
i: Mass assignment is the same issue (OWASP API3: broken object property level authorization).
Response DTOs prevent the reverse: excessive data exposure.
Integration test sending {"status":"Delivered","isAdmin":true} to verify extra fields are ignored.
System.Text.Json UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow (.NET 8) can reject unknown fields entirely.
f: Is [Bind] enough?
It works but is easy to forget; DTOs are clearer.
How do you test for it?
Send extra fields and assert they're ignored.
